arrival.note: HURLBUT PRINTS THE SENTENCE, AND IT IS HURLBUT'S OWN AND NOT HUBBARD'S. Chicago Antiquities (1881) pages 28-36: "Mr. Hubbard left Montreal, were his parents then lived, May 13, 1818, reaching Mackinaw, July 4 and first arrived at Chicago on the last day of October or first day of November of that year" (bk_afc_004; data/research/books/text/hurlbut_chicago_antiquities_28_36.txt lines 31-34). THE VALUE IS THE EARLIER OF THE TWO DAYS THE SOURCE OFFERS AND THE PRECISION SAYS SO: the page gives 31 October OR 1 November and refuses to choose between them, so this record refuses too - `day` would pick one on the reader's behalf and `year` would throw away a reading that is exact to within a day. WHY THIS IS GRADED INFERRED AND NOT ATTESTED. The sentence stands OUTSIDE the quotation marks that open four lines later at 'Having entire charge of the management of the company in the West' - it is Henry H. Hurlbut compiling in 1881, sixty-three years after the day and forty-six after the scene, not Gurdon Hubbard remembering in his own voice. data/sources/chicago_antiquities_american_fur_co.json grades that layer rung 4 and says in terms that nothing taken from Hurlbut's own narrative may be used as if it were period evidence; the source record's tier of 1 is earned by the 1821-22 invoice book alone and is not a licence over the compiler's prose. So the day is cited rather than conjectured, and it is still one man's account of another man's boyhood at second hand. It REPLACES the conjecture this record used to carry - 'NOT ATTESTED IN ANYTHING WORKED FOR THIS PARCEL... carried as a conjecture citing nothing and flagged for a later parcel to fix or delete' - which named the commonplace of the Chicago literature and no sentence (T-0594, closing what T-0575's crosswalk deferred). Arriving in 1818 is not residing here in 1835: the residence claim is unchanged and rests where it always did, on the trusteeship and the town's own rolls.

origin.note: THE OTHER HALF OF THE ARRIVAL THIS RECORD ALREADY CARRIES. Hurlbut's chapter gives the departure with its date - "Mr. Hubbard left Montreal, were his parents then lived, May 13, 1818" - and the sentence before it gives the birth - "He was born in Windsor, Vt., in 1802" (bk_afc_004; data/research/books/text/hurlbut_chicago_antiquities_28_36.txt lines 32-33). The birthplace is there a second time and from the man himself: the Calumet Club's register of 27 May 1879 prints a BIRTHPLACE column, and his entry reads "Hubbard, Gurdon S. | 1818, Oct. 1, | Windsor, Vt. | 76 | 243 White St., Chicago." (os1879r078, data/research/old_settlers/people.json). WHY MONTREAL IS THE VALUE AND WINDSOR IS IN IT TOO. `origin` is where a household came FROM, and this corpus writes the route rather than one place wherever a source gives one - hh_maxwell_philip.json reads "Sackett's Harbor, New York; born at Guilford, Vermont" for the same shape of life. Hubbard left from Montreal and was born at Windsor; the semicolon holds the two apart rather than letting a birthplace pass for a departure. HE DID NOT ARRIVE AS A HOUSEHOLD, AND THIS FIELD DOES NOT SAY HE DID. He came at sixteen as one of the clerks the American Fur Company brought from Montreal to Mackinaw in 1817-18, seventeen years before the scene, and `party_size_on_arrival` stays null because the source counts nobody with him. The `arrival` above already carries the end of that same journey, at this grade and for this reason (T-0594); its origin is the other half of one claim and not a second one. THE GRADE IS THE SENTENCE'S AND NOT THE MAN'S: the passage stands outside the quotation marks that open four lines later at "Having entire charge of the management of the company in the West", so it is Henry H. Hurlbut compiling in 1881, which data/sources/chicago_antiquities_american_fur_co.json grades rung 4 and forbids being used as period evidence; the 1879 register is the man's own recollection at sixty years' distance, which under the ratified ladder (T-0513) corroborates and dates and cannot lift a rung. HIS PARENTS ARE NAMED AND ARE NOT MINTED: "parents were Elizur and Abigail (Sage) Hubbard", who were living at Montreal in 1818. Nothing this project holds puts either of them in Chicago on any date, so they are recorded here in prose and nowhere as persons of a town they are not attested in (T-0753).

persons.name: Gurdon Saltonstall Hubbard

birth_year.note: "He was born in Windsor, Vt., in 1802" - Hurlbut, Chicago Antiquities (1881), pages 28-36 (bk_afc_004; data/research/books/text/hurlbut_chicago_antiquities_28_36.txt line 32). A SECOND SOURCE AGREES WITHOUT BEING ASKED, and it is the man himself: the Calumet Club's Old Settlers' register of 27 May 1879 records his age as 76 (os1879r078), which puts the birth between 28 May 1802 and 27 May 1803 and contains the printed year; its BIRTHPLACE column gives "Windsor, Vt." for the second time. INFERRED AND NOT ATTESTED, on whose voice the sentence is in. It stands outside the quotation marks that open four lines later, so it is the compiler writing in 1881 and data/sources/chicago_antiquities_american_fur_co.json grades that layer rung 4; the register is a recollection set down sixty years after the fact, which under the ratified ladder (T-0513) corroborates and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself. NO AGE IS WRITTEN FOR THE SCENE DATE. A year without a day makes this man 32 or 33 on 1 July 1835 and no source here gives the month, so a single number would pick one of the two on the reader's behalf - the same refusal the arrival's `either_of_two_days` precision makes on this record already. The chapter's own "then a youth of sixteen" for May 1818 is the compiler's round figure beside his own printed year and is not read as a second date (T-0753).

occupation.note: A forwarding and packing merchant. data/structures/old_bank_building.json records that he packed there in the 1834 season; Andreas's chapter heading calls him 'Gurdon S. Hubbard, the oldest living resident of Chicago' and he supplied Andreas with the Ramsey Crooks correspondence on the early fur trade.

persons.note: ELECTED A TRUSTEE OF THE TOWN AT THE SECOND ELECTION, 11 AUGUST 1834 - 'J. H. Kinzie, G. S. Hubbard, E. Goodrich, J. K. Boyer, and John S. C. Hogan were chosen Trustees' - so he is on the board through the municipal year that ends in the scene month. He is also the man whose 1881 correction of the Wau-Bun view of Fort Dearborn supplies four of the constraints this project's fort dossier rests on: that the enclosure ran 'nearly north and south, east and west', that the north picket line stood nowhere more than 80 ft from the water, that the ground at the fort was 'not over eight feet above the River at its lowest stage', and that the north and south gates were on one sight line. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Hubbard, Gurdon S.” (tax_1833_046, line 98); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Hubbard, G. S.” (poll_1834_055, line 224). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Hubbard' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). OLD SETTLERS, 1879 — A DATE THIS MAN GAVE FOR HIMSELF, AND STILL NOT A FACT ABOUT 1835. The Calumet Club's FIRST reception to the settlers of Chicago prior to 1840, 27 May 1879, printed its register in the proceedings (Early Chicago, Chicago, 1879, pages 84-90), and this man's entry reads “Hubbard, Gurdon S. | 1818, Oct. 1, | Windsor, Vt. | 76 | 243 White St., Chicago.” — name, his own date of arrival, his birthplace, his age and his 1879 post-office address, in the register's five columns. The date of arrival is HIS RECOLLECTION, set down forty to sixty years after the event; the address is where he lived in 1879 and is never read as an 1835 residence. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a later recollection corroborates, enriches and dates and cannot lift a rung by itself, so this record's GRADE IS UNCHANGED by it: T-0513 consolidates the identity and T-0515 regrades. Identity by rule OS1 — surname and spelled-out forename agree, one bearer (data/research/old_settlers/crosswalk.json).

research_note: THE OLDEST LIVING RESIDENT, AND THE ONE HOUSEHOLD IN THE PARCEL WHOSE ARRIVAL DATE THIS PROJECT HAD TO REFUSE TO GUESS - UNTIL A SENTENCE TURNED UP. Everything about Hubbard's later Chicago life was documented here and the date he first came was a fact everyone knew and nothing in data/sources/ stated, so it was carried as a conjecture citing nothing and left visibly empty rather than quietly filled: it was the case AGENTS.md rule 1 exists for. Hurlbut's American Fur Company chapter, read for T-0575 and cited by this record since T-0594, closes it - Montreal 13 May 1818, Mackinaw 4 July, Chicago the last day of October or the first of November - and the asymmetry that was worth leaving visible is now a smaller and more interesting one. The sentence is the COMPILER'S, not the man's: it stands outside the quotation marks in which Hubbard speaks four lines later, so a date this project had no source for at all now has a source of 1881 at rung 4, and the record says both things on its face rather than letting the citation look like an attestation.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints.
